planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in full sun to light shade and well-drained soil.

directions: Selected and introduced by the U.S. National Arboretum, this fountain grass forms a graceful, spreading clump of glossy dark green foliage that colors yellow-orange in autumn. Its dark purple, bottlebrush-like plumes emerge later in the season than most fountain grass cultivars, so it extends bloom interest into early fall when many companion grasses have already finished flowering. The cultivar shows notable resistance to verticillium wilt, a soilborne disease that can trouble other Pennisetum selections planted in heavier or previously infected soils. Cut the clump back hard in late winter before new shoots emerge to keep the mound tidy and encourage fresh growth.
sources: Kansas State University Research and Extension

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in full sun and average, well-drained soil.

directions: Bred by Brent Horvath at Intrinsic Perennial Gardens and introduced in 2013, 'Ginger Love' produces unusually thick, bushy, reddish-purple flower spikes that appear in mid to late summer well above the mounded green foliage and persist into winter. Foliage shifts from green to yellow in early fall before settling into a soft coppery bronze, adding a second season of color after the plumes fade to beige. Its compact, uniform habit and drought tolerance suit it to mass plantings, mixed borders, or large containers where a bold textural accent is wanted. Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new growth resumes to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in full sun to partial shade and well-drained soil.

directions: This tidy, tufted evergreen grass rolls its narrow leaves so that the dark green upper surface and powdery blue underside show at once, producing a distinctive two-toned sheen that intensifies to solid blue by summer and holds through winter. Chocolate-brown flower spikes tipped with buttery yellow anthers appear on short stems in very early spring, ahead of most other ornamental grasses. It is highly adaptable to average garden soil and tolerates both heat and drought once established, making it useful as an edging along paths or as a transition planting between lawn and border. Comb out old foliage in late winter to refresh the clump before new blue growth emerges.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in full sun to light shade and moderately fertile, well-drained soil.

directions: Discovered as a chance seedling at John Greenlee's Southern California nursery and thought to combine traits of Sesleria autumnalis and Sesleria caerulea, this compact grass forms a dense mound of fine, rich blue-green blades that hold their color through most of the year. Pale purple flower spikes rise just above the foliage in spring and early summer, maturing to purplish-brown seed heads that add subtle texture without becoming weedy or self-sowing. It stays neat with minimal care, tolerating both moist and fairly dry well-drained sites, and combines well with other small grasses or as a repeating groundcover element in a meadow-style planting. Shear back lightly in late winter only if foliage looks tattered, since the clump otherwise remains attractive with little maintenance.
